## Merge vs Rebase

**Merge** — join branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  (main)
     \     \
      D---E--M  (merge commit)
```

**Rebase** — replay commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C---D'---E'  (rebased)
```

---

## Use Merge When

- Public/shared branch (never rebase shared history)
- Want preserve exact what happened, when
- PR merge into main → standard practice
- Reverting easier with explicit merge commit

## Use Rebase When

- Local feature branch, not yet pushed
- Want clean linear history before PR
- `git pull --rebase` to avoid noise merge commits on fast pull
- Squash messy WIP commits before review

---

## Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | True, messy | Clean, rewritten |
| Conflict | Resolve once | Resolve per commit |
| Safe on shared? | Yes | **No** |
| Blame/bisect | Harder | Easy |
| Revert | Clear target | Can revert individual replayed commits |

---

## Golden Rule

> Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch.

Rebase rewrites SHA hashes. Others have old SHAs → chaos, force-push required, teammates hate you.

---

## Quick Decision

- On own feature branch, cleaning up? → **rebase**
- Merging feature into main/dev? → **merge**
- Pulling latest from main into feature? → `git pull --rebase` or `git fetch + git rebase origin/main`
- Anything public/shared? → **merge, always**
